newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil government set back in civil service reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil government set back in civil service reform.

text.p: A defeat for the Brazilian government in a vote on amendments to a civil service reform bill represents a serious blow to its attempts to streamline the state bureaucracy, officials and lawmakers said.
In the Chamber of Deputies Wednesday evening, the government fell 10 votes short of the three-fifths majority needed to turn back an amendment floated by the left-wing Workers Party (PT).
The amendment removes a clause in the reform bill that would have created a category of public sector worker whose jobs would not have been protected by the constitution.

Currently, civil servants who follow public sector hiring procedure and serve two years in their posts cannot be fired, making it difficult for central and local governments to reduce the burden of payroll spending.

As well as maintaining the single category for all civil servants, the amendment also struck down a proposal in the reform bill that would have gradually reduced the number of bonuses that could be earned by public sector workers.
"Damage has been done but it hasn't sunk the reform. For the time being, it's still afloat," said a congressional official who has been working on the bill.
Deputy Marcelo Deda of the Workers Party said the defeat was a major blow to the government which the opposition hoped to repeat in voting on other amendments to the reform legislation.
One of those amendments seeks to strike down an article allowing the government to dismiss workers whose jobs are currently protected by the constitution.
"A column has been demolished and now the whole structure is wobbling," Deda said.

The civil service reform is considered crucial to Brazil's attempts to rein in public spending but has been hampered by opposition from left-wing political parties, trade unions and members of the government's own mulitparty alliance.
A latest crisis blew up earlier this month when the government withdrew its support for an amendment that would have exempted members of Congress from a proposed pay ceiling.
The government had said it would support the amendment only hours before the civil service reform bill itself was put to its first vote in the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress.
The bill passed by 309 votes, just one vote more than the three-fifths majority it needed.
The lower house has not yet voted on the amendment to exempt members of Congress from the pay ceiling.
Sensing a rebellion among government-allied deputies after the U-turn on the exemption, government whips had sought to avoid voting on any amendments that threatened key points of the reform bill.

But on Wednesday Vice President Marco Maciel told the whips to press ahead with voting on some amendments, local newspapers said. He was standing in for President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, who is in Canada.

Seeking to win back the support of disgruntled deputies, the whips agreed to cut an article that would have ended the current practice of awarding public sector pensioners all pay rises given to active workers. The article was one of several opposed by the so-called "pensioners lobby" in Congress. Those lawmakers earn handsome pensions from previous public sector posts on top of their salaries of 8,000 reais ($7,547).
Smarting from the defeat on Wednesday, whips were reported to favor suspending further voting on important amendments for two weeks.
